config.title: color-scheme

intro.title: color-scheme
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple webpage that automatically adapts its color scheme to match your system's light or dark mode preference. You will learn the core concept of the CSS `color-scheme` property, which allows you to control how the browser renders default UI elements like form controls and scrollbars. The main technology involved is CSS, using this property to ensure visual consistency. By the end, you'll understand how to implement `color-scheme` to create a more seamless user experience across different system settings.
intro.usecase: The color-scheme property is essential for creating accessible applications that respect user preferences across operating systems and browsers. Developers use it to ensure form controls, dropdown menus, and scrollbars automatically match the user's chosen light or dark mode in settings panels, admin dashboards, and data visualization tools. This eliminates manual theming for native UI components in complex interfaces like analytics platforms or content management systems, providing consistent visual experiences while reducing development overhead.

objectives: Apply the color-scheme property to HTML elements to control their rendering mode
Configure color-scheme values to match system preferences or enforce specific themes
Manipulate form controls and other components to respect the declared color scheme
Integrate color-scheme with CSS custom properties for consistent theming
Construct media queries that respond to user preference and adjust color-scheme accordingly
Initialize a document-wide color scheme that cascades to all child elements
Update existing CSS rules to be compatible with both light and dark color schemes

steps.title: Create a basic HTML structure to apply CSS color-scheme
steps.instruction: Create an HTML file with a basic structure including head and body sections, and link a CSS file named 'styles.css'.
steps.hint: Start with the <!DOCTYPE html> declaration, then create <html>, <head>, and <body> elements. Inside <head>, add a <link> element to connect your CSS file.
steps.analogousExample:
<!-- Basic HTML structure with linked CSS -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>
<body>
    <!-- Content will go here -->
</body>
</html>

steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a valid HTML document structure ready to apply CSS color-scheme properties.
successCriteria: The HTML file includes proper doctype, html, head, and body elements with a link to 'styles.css'.

steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you have all required elements: doctype, html, head with CSS link, and body.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that your HTML structure includes the basic elements and properly links the CSS file.

steps.title: Create the CSS file and link it to HTML
steps.instruction: Create a new CSS file named 'styles.css' and link it in the HTML head section using a <link> element.
steps.hint: Use a <link> tag with rel='stylesheet' and href='styles.css' inside the <head> section.
steps.analogousExample:
<!-- Linking a CSS file -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
steps.seedCode:
Color Scheme Demo

This text will adapt to light or dark mode.
steps.expectedOutcome: The HTML file now includes a link to an external CSS file, establishing the styling environment.
successCriteria: A <link> element with rel='stylesheet' and href='styles.css' is added to the <head> section.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but ensure the <link> tag has both rel='stylesheet' and href='styles.css' attributes.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS file isn't properly linked. Check that you added a <link> element in the <head> with the correct attributes.

steps.title: Apply basic styling to HTML elements
steps.instruction: In your CSS file, add rules to style the background, text color, and borders for the .demo-container, h1, p, button, form, label, and input elements.
steps.hint: Use CSS selectors like .demo-container, h1, p, button, form, label, and input. Set properties like background-color, color, border, padding, and margin.
steps.expectedOutcome: The HTML elements will have visible styles applied, creating a foundation that will later respond to color-scheme changes.
successCriteria: CSS rules are added for .demo-container, h1, p, button, form, label, and input with at least background-color, color, and border properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some styles, but make sure to style all the elements: .demo-container, h1, p, button, form, label, and input with background, text, and border properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: No CSS rules were added. Please add styles for the elements to create a visual foundation.

steps.title: Introduce the color-scheme property on the root element
steps.instruction: In your CSS file, add a rule for the :root selector and set the color-scheme property to 'normal'.
steps.hint: The :root selector targets the root element of the document. Use the property color-scheme with the value 'normal'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The color-scheme property is applied to the root element, setting the default color scheme for the entire document.
successCriteria: The CSS file contains a :root selector with the color-scheme property set to 'normal'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the :root selector and setting color-scheme to 'normal'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've added a rule for :root with the color-scheme property set to 'normal'.

steps.title: Apply color-scheme: light to specific elements
steps.instruction: Create a CSS class named .light-scheme that applies color-scheme: light to elements.
steps.hint: Define a class selector starting with a dot, then add the color-scheme property with the value 'light'.
steps.expectedOutcome: A CSS class .light-scheme is defined with color-scheme: light.
successCriteria: The .light-scheme class is created and includes color-scheme: light.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined a class named .light-scheme with color-scheme: light.
steps.feedbackWrong: The class wasn't created correctly. Check the syntax and property value.

steps.title: Apply color-scheme: dark to specific elements
steps.instruction: Create a CSS class named .dark-scheme that applies color-scheme: dark.
steps.hint: Define a new CSS class starting with a dot, then set the color-scheme property to dark.
steps.expectedOutcome: A .dark-scheme class is defined with color-scheme: dark, ready to be applied to HTML elements.
successCriteria: The .dark-scheme class exists and sets color-scheme: dark.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the class is named .dark-scheme and includes color-scheme: dark.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the instruction: you need to define a CSS class with color-scheme: dark.

steps.title: Use prefers-color-scheme media query with color-scheme
steps.instruction: Create a media query for prefers-color-scheme: light that sets color-scheme: light on the :root element.
steps.hint: Use @media (prefers-color-scheme: light) { ... } to target systems with light mode preference.
steps.expectedOutcome: The :root element will automatically use light color scheme when the system preference is set to light mode.
successCriteria: A media query for prefers-color-scheme: light exists and sets color-scheme: light on :root.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your media query targets prefers-color-scheme: light and sets color-scheme: light on :root.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. Create a media query using @media (prefers-color-scheme: light) that sets color-scheme: light on the :root element.

steps.title: Demonstrate color-scheme inheritance and override behavior
steps.instruction: Create a nested div inside the .light-scheme element and give it a class .nested-dark that sets color-scheme: dark to demonstrate overriding.
steps.hint: Add a new CSS rule for .nested-dark inside your existing .light-scheme rule or after it.
steps.expectedOutcome: The learner will create a CSS rule that demonstrates how color-scheme can be overridden in nested elements.
successCriteria: A CSS rule for .nested-dark is created that sets color-scheme: dark and is nested inside .light-scheme.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your .nested-dark rule sets color-scheme: dark and is properly nested inside .light-scheme.
steps.feedbackWrong: The nested override rule isn't quite right. Check that you've created .nested-dark with color-scheme: dark inside .light-scheme.

steps.title: Test and observe color-scheme effects on form controls and system colors
steps.instruction: Add CSS rules to style form controls (input, button, select) and observe how they respond to different color-scheme values.
steps.hint: Style form elements with borders, backgrounds, and text colors to see how color-scheme affects their default system appearance.
steps.expectedOutcome: Form controls will be styled to clearly show how color-scheme affects their system colors and appearance.
successCriteria: Form controls (input, button, select) are styled with CSS properties that demonstrate color-scheme effects.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some styling, but make sure to style multiple form controls (input, button, select) to fully observe color-scheme effects.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try adding CSS rules that style form controls like input, button, and select to see how color-scheme affects them.
